## Highlights [...] Taking a broader view of 2026 shows the price effects from last year’s tariff increases appear to be fading. At its peak in late-2025, goods prices (excluding food & energy) were running at an annualized rate of 1.5% and were contributing 0.4 percentage points to core inflation. Today, its contribution has slowed to about half of that, while the share of goods categories registering price growth has narrowed considerably (Chart 4).

results.content: In the second quarter of 2026, US consumers faced uneven hiring, rising inflation, and ongoing geopolitical tensions. Against that backdrop, a smaller share of consumers reported feeling more optimistic about the economy, while a greater share said they felt pessimistic. Consumers also reported intentions to pull back spending across most discretionary categories.
